name: Glute bridges / glute activation

lead: Lying on your back with bent knees, you lift the hips by squeezing the glutes. It builds glute strength and size, and in posture circles it is used to counter anterior pelvic tilt for less lower-back arch.

The glutes extend the hip, and proponents say strengthening them helps hold the pelvis in a more neutral position. Wikipedia lists it among suggested exercises for pelvic tilt but flags the sourcing as weak; no trial tests it for pelvic tilt or looks.

paras: People do bodyweight bridges as sets of repetitions or as a low-load activation drill before heavier training, usually as part of a routine with hip flexor stretching and core work.
No specific harms are documented for bodyweight bridges. Back or hip pain is typically referred to a clinician.

angle.text: Glute bridges strengthen the glutes and, in posture circles, are used to pull the pelvis toward neutral for a flatter lower-back line. They also build glute size. Research covers muscle activation, not pelvic tilt or looks.

lead: The glute bridge is a floor exercise in which a person lies on their back with knees bent and lifts the hips by contracting the gluteal and hamstring muscles. Related bridge exercises are described by Wikipedia as intended to improve lower back and gluteus strength [1]. People use it to build and wake up the glutes, which form the prominence of the buttocks and are widely seen as part of an athletic, well-proportioned physique [2].

The term glute activation refers to low-load drills such as bridges, clamshells and banded walks done before heavier training to switch on the gluteal muscles. T Nation training logs show lifters using single-leg glute bridges in warm-ups and as a way to find out whether the glutes are working [3][4].

In looksmaxxing and posture communities the glute bridge is also listed as a counter to anterior pelvic tilt, on the idea that weak glutes allow the pelvis to tip forward, giving a more upright stance and a flatter-looking lower back. Wikipedia's article on pelvic tilt lists glute bridges among recommended exercises, but flags that part of the article as relying on a consumer-health source [5].
infobox: Anterior pelvic tilt correction, couch stretch

paras: Bridge exercises are described as engaging the lower back, gluteus muscles and hips, along with the hamstrings and quadriceps. Common variants include a static hold and single-leg versions that increase the load on the hamstrings and glutes. The related gymnastic bridge is a distinct, more demanding movement [1].

The gluteus maximus is the largest muscle in the body and the main hip extender; Wikipedia lists hip thrusts, glute bridges, squats, deadlifts, kettlebell swings and lunges as exercises that target it, and notes that squats produce high levels of gluteal activation [2].

The gluteus maximus is the main hip extensor and the largest muscle in the human body; its thick mass forms the prominence of the buttocks.[2] It arises from the outer ilium, the sacrum and coccyx, and nearby fascia, and inserts mainly into the iliotibial band and the gluteal tuberosity of the femur.[2] When the hip is flexed, it extends the leg back in line with the body, and its most powerful action is to return the body upright after stooping by drawing the pelvis backward, assisted by the hamstrings and adductor magnus.[2]

Wikipedia notes that the human gluteus maximus is about 1.6 times larger relative to body mass than a chimpanzee's, and that evidence suggests its enlargement relates more to running and trunk stabilization than to walking, in which the muscle shows little activity.[2] The glute bridge trains hip extension from the floor with the trunk supported, so the effort falls on the glutes and hamstrings with the spinal erectors stabilizing.[1][2]

Wikipedia's list of exercises that target the gluteus maximus includes hip thrusts, glute bridges, quadruped hip extensions, kettlebell swings, squats and their variations, lunges, deadlifts, reverse hyperextensions, four-way hip extensions and glute-ham raises.[2] The bridge is the simplest of these because it needs only a floor, which is why it is used as a beginner movement, a warm-up and a form of active recovery. Training logs on T Nation show it in a circuit of bodyweight squats, push-ups and mountain climbers as active recovery,[6] and in morning warm-ups beside banded box walks and clamshells.[4]

Common progressions described in these logs and in the encyclopedic sources are the single-leg bridge, the loaded bridge with a weight on the hips, banded versions and the elevated hip thrust with the upper back on a bench.[1][2][4]
The gluteus maximus forms the prominence of the buttocks, and Wikipedia notes that strong, well-developed glutes are often seen as healthy and aesthetically appealing [2].

Posture sources describe the pelvic tilt pattern as hip flexors shortening while hip extensors, including the glutes, lengthen. Strengthening the glutes is therefore commonly paired with hip flexor stretching and core work [5][7]. Wikipedia notes that exercise recommendations in these articles are thinly referenced [5][7].

Wikipedia notes that the glutes are often regarded as a symbol of health and strength and as aesthetically appealing, with depictions of prominent, well-proportioned gluteal muscles in art from Ancient Greece to the present.[2] In fitness culture this underlies the popularity of glute-focused programs, and in posture and looksmaxxing circles the same muscle is discussed for its role in the pelvis and lower back.

Posture advocates connect weak or inactive glutes with sitting-heavy lifestyles. A T Nation member who attributed a weakly firing glute to long hours of sitting and driving reported a big change after short sets repeated across the day,[8] and another credited glute activation after a chiropractor visit for relief of pain when squatting.[9]

On T Nation, lifters describe using glute bridges to test glute engagement. One member advised another who could not feel the glutes working to try sets of bridges, with single-leg versions if strong enough, while noting that single-leg work made the other's hamstrings cramp [3]. Another member reported that a chiropractor found a weak, non-firing left glute and that repeated short sets across the day made a large difference [8]. Glute activation drills such as banded walks, clamshells and single-leg bridges also appear in lifters' warm-up routines [4][9].

Wikipedia cites a 2016 study in the Journal of Physical Therapy Science on trunk and hip extensor muscle activity during bridge exercises with varied unilateral knee angles, but its findings are not reported there [1]. That research concerns muscle activation, not pelvic alignment or appearance.

Wikipedia's pelvic tilt and lordosis articles describe anterior pelvic tilt as associated with shortened hip flexors and lengthened extensors and list glute strengthening among suggested exercises, while the pages are marked as thinly referenced; clinicians commonly refer persistent back or hip pain for assessment, and functional tests such as the 30-second chair-to-stand are used in rehabilitation settings to assess lower-limb strength.[5][7][2]
No studies found on glute bridges as a pelvic tilt or appearance intervention. Related laboratory work on muscle activity during bridge variations exists but did not measure those outcomes [1].
